growth_story.headline: Peru's income per person grew 5.3 percent a year in the 2002–2013 commodity boom; since 2014 it has grown 1.3 percent a year amid political turmoil.
growth_story.arc: Peru entered the 1990s in collapse: income per person fell 11.5 percent in 1988, 14.3 percent in 1989 and 7.1 percent in 1990, as hyperinflation took hold. A stabilization program in 1990–92 and later reforms brought growth back, but the first era, 1990–2001, averaged only 1.0 percent a year, with a new fall in 1998 that the IMF calls a reminder of Peru's exposure to external shocks. From 2002 to 2013 income per person grew 5.3 percent a year in what the World Bank calls a commodity boom, and investment climbed to 25.3 percent of GDP by 2013. Growth then slowed sharply in 2014, and the era since has averaged 1.3 percent a year; the World Bank links this to high political volatility and the IMF to a fall in productivity growth. The pandemic cut income per person by 12.0 percent in 2020, and climate shocks and social unrest brought another fall of 1.4 percent in 2023, yet by 2025 income per person was at its highest level so far.

threads.title: Stabilization after hyperinflation
threads.text: In the late 1980s output collapsed and prices spun out of control. A stabilization program in 1990–92 took on the crisis and began a long run of reforms, but growth in the 1990s stayed uneven, and 1998 brought a new fall.

threads.title: The commodity boom years
threads.text: From 2002 to 2013 income per person grew 5.3 percent a year, in what the World Bank calls a commodity boom. The boom ended in 2014, when the economy slowed more sharply than at any time since the global financial crisis.

citations.title: Peru’s Road to Economic Success

threads.title: Political volatility
threads.text: Since the boom ended, Peru has gone through repeated changes of president. The World Bank links this turmoil to the slower growth of the past decade, and the IMF counts political uncertainty and social unrest among the main risks at home.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Peru (October 2026)
citations.quote: Over the past decade, Peru’s high political volatility—marked by eight changes in the presidency—held average real annual GDP growth to 2.5 percent

citations.title: Peru: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2026 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Key domestic risks: political uncertainty, social unrest, weather-related shocks including a stronger El Niño Costero, persistently high insecurity, and illegal mining.

threads.title: Slow productivity, wide informality
threads.text: The IMF finds that slower productivity growth has pulled down how fast the economy can grow. Most workers hold informal jobs, and the World Bank says this, along with weak public services and gaps in infrastructure, has held back growth.

citations.title: Peru: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2024 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Average and potential growth have fallen to about 2.5 percent, driven by a decline in total factor productivity growth

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Peru (October 2026)
citations.quote: High worker informality, around 70 percent, poor public service delivery, and infrastructure deficiencies, have damped growth potential.

threads.title: Weather shocks and export prices
threads.text: Climate shocks and social unrest pushed income per person down in 2023. Since then export prices at record highs against import prices have pulled the other way, while a new El Niño has hit farming and fishing.

citations.title: Peru: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2024 Article IV Mission

citations.title: Peru: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2026 Article IV Mission

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Peru (October 2026)

since_last_year.text: In 2025 income per person grew 2.4 percent and reached a new high, and the IMF reports private investment growing at its fastest pace since 2013, leaving aside the rebound after the pandemic. In 2026 a new government took office after the election and business expectations rose, while an El Niño event weighed on farming and fishing.

citations.title: Peru: Staff Concluding Statement of the 2026 Article IV Mission
citations.quote: Private investment grew 10 percent in 2025, its strongest pace since 2013 excluding the post-pandemic rebound.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Peru (October 2026)
citations.quote: The 2026 election brought in a new administration whose stated priorities include supporting public and private investment, which immediately lifted business expectations

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Peru (October 2026)
citations.quote: El Niño Costero weighed on agricultural and fisheries output, but exceptionally favorable terms of trade supported strong performance

growth_story.tension: The sources describe the decade since the boom in terms of total GDP growth, but income per person grew only 1.3 percent a year over 2014–2025, because part of the growth went to a larger population. And while the IMF reports private investment in 2025 growing at its fastest pace since 2013, investment was still 20.5 percent of GDP in 2025, below the 25.3 percent of 2013.
